doc: Arrival-time and service-fact formatting rules. These are DOMAIN RULES, not wire shapes: no schema can generate them, so every platform hand-ports them and this corpus is the only thing that keeps the ports equal. Read the file, iterate `groups`, run each case, compare to `expect`. Conventions used throughout this directory: (1) JSON `null` means the language's absent value (TS `undefined`, Swift `nil`, Kotlin `null`) both in arguments and in `expect`; (2) `nowIso` is the clock reading, passed in because every rule here is pure; (3) arrivals are ISO-8601 with a fixed +08:00 offset, so lexical order is chronological; (4) `knownDefect: true` marks a case that records what the code does today and is AGREED to be wrong — see `note`. A defect row is not permission to diverge: fix it in every platform at once, in the same commit that edits the row. ETAs are approximations (ADR-008) — no rule here fabricates sub-minute precision.

etaView.doc: Signed seconds/minutes to arrival plus the two honesty flags. `minutes` is FLOORED, so it reads as whole minutes still remaining (countdown-board convention): 119 s is '1 min', not '2 min'. `isDue` is a symmetric +/-60 s window around the arrival, so a feed whose clock is a little behind still says 'Due' instead of flipping to a departed dash. Anything earlier than -60 s has departed.

cases.name: minute-boundary-119s
cases.why: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW. One second under two minutes. Floor gives 1, so the label stays '1 min'. A port that rounds instead of floors shows '2 min' here and overstates the wait by a whole minute.

cases.name: minute-boundary-120s
cases.why: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW. Exactly two minutes — the first second at which the label reads '2 min'.

cases.name: minute-boundary-121s
cases.why: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW. One second past two minutes — still '2 min'. Together with the two rows above this pins the whole rounding rule with three cases.

cases.name: due-window-upper-edge-59s
cases.why: Last second inside the 'Due' window.

cases.name: first-numeric-second-60s
cases.why: The first second that shows a number rather than 'Due'.

cases.name: due-window-lower-edge-minus-60s
cases.why: 60 s in the past is still 'Due', not departed — the tolerance band for feed clock skew. Note `minutes` is -1 because the floor of -1.0 is -1.

cases.name: first-departed-second-minus-61s
cases.why: One second past the tolerance band. `minutes` is -2, not -1: flooring a negative goes away from zero (floor(-61/60) = -2). A port using integer truncation gets -1 here and will disagree.

cases.name: a-served-due-threshold-moves-both-flags
cases.why: The threshold is served policy (ADR-053), and this row is why it is ONE number rather than two: 40 s out is inside the shipped 60 s band but outside a served 30 s one, so `isDue` goes false — and the same 30 s must simultaneously govern the departed side, which the second half of this row's clock reading fixes at -40 s. A port holding its own constant reads both flags wrongly here and correctly everywhere else in the group.

cases.name: a-served-due-threshold-shortens-the-tolerance-band
cases.why: The departed half of the row above, at the same served 30 s: a bus 40 s in the past is gone under a 30 s tolerance, where the shipped 60 s would still show it. Pinned as its own row because the pair is the whole symmetry, and a port that applied the override to `isDue` but left `hasDeparted` on its own constant passes the row above and fails this one.

cases.name: unparseable-arrival-is-departed
cases.why: GUARD ROW (ADR-142). The wire admits any string and cleanArrivals drops only falsy values, so a malformed operator timestamp reaches this function. NaN seconds used to fail every band and render a literal 'NaN min' in the normal colour on every readout in the product. The one honest arm every consumer already has is 'departed' (formatRelative's dash, etaLabelParts' departed, etaUrgency's none, upcoming's filter), so an unreadable arrival takes it. The zeros are a defined sentinel, not a measurement: JSON cannot hold NaN, and no caller reads the figures once hasDeparted is true.

formatRelative.doc: The rider-facing relative label. Under a minute it is a word, never a number. A departed bus is an em dash, never a negative number. Between 60 s and 119 s it is '1 min' (the value is clamped to at least 1, so the numeric slot never shows 0).

cases.name: minute-boundary-119s-en
cases.why: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW, label side: 119 s reads '1 min'.

cases.name: clamped-to-one-minute-at-60s
cases.why: 60 s..119 s all read '1 min'. The clamp exists so the badge never renders a bare '0'.

cases.name: departed-is-an-em-dash-not-a-number
cases.why: U+2014 EM DASH. Never a negative minute count.

cases.name: unparseable-arrival-is-the-dash
cases.why: The rendered half of etaView's guard row: an arrival that cannot be read shows the departed dash, never 'NaN min' (ADR-142).

etaLabelParts.doc: The same rule as formatRelative, split so a caller can render the number large and the unit small and pinned — only the digits move as the value changes. Three variants; the discriminator is `kind`. The last two rows carry an explicit `dueUnderSec`: the parameter had been missing, so `EtaBadge` — the only caller — silently ignored a served ClientPolicy while every other caller of `etaView` honoured it (ADR-053; closed in WP4-0).

cases.name: departed-carries-no-label
cases.why: The departed variant has no text at all — the caller decides how to render an absence, so no platform invents a string here.

cases.name: served-due-band-narrows-what-counts-as-due
cases.why: A served `dueUnderSec` of 30 makes a 45 s arrival a figure rather than "Due". Under the shipped 60 s default the same reading is "Due", so this row fails against any implementation that drops the parameter — which is exactly what the code did before WP4-0.

cases.name: served-due-band-also-moves-the-departed-edge
cases.why: The band is symmetric — one number for "no figure yet" and "still worth showing" (see etaView). With `dueUnderSec: 30`, a bus 45 s in the PAST is departed, where the 60 s default still shows it as Due. Pins that a port threads the override into both halves, not just the forward one.

cases.name: unparseable-arrival-is-departed
cases.why: The badge half of etaView's guard row: kind 'departed', never {kind:'mins', value:NaN} (ADR-142).

formatClock.doc: Hong Kong wall-clock time of an arrival, `HH:mm` on a 24-hour clock, zero-padded on both fields. Takes NO locale: a 24-hour HH:mm is identical in all three of ours, so a locale argument could only introduce a difference nobody wants. Two properties are the whole point of this group. First, the output depends on the INSTANT and nothing else — not on the device time zone, not on the host's ICU version — so a `Z` input and the same instant written `+08:00` must render identically, and a rider in London sees Hong Kong time on a Hong Kong bus board. Second, sub-minute precision is TRUNCATED, never rounded up (ADR-008): 12:05:59.999 is '12:05'. This function previously used `toLocaleTimeString`, whose output no corpus could pin because it was a property of the machine rather than of the rule; it is arithmetic now, which is what makes these rows meaningful.

cases.name: hk-offset-input
cases.why: The everyday case: the offset our feeds actually carry.

cases.name: utc-input-renders-as-hong-kong-time
cases.why: THE ROW THAT MATTERS. The same instant as the row above, written in UTC. A port that formats with the device zone gets '04:05' here on a UTC machine and '00:05' in New York — the failure mode this function was rewritten to remove.

cases.name: non-hk-offset-input-renders-as-hong-kong-time
cases.why: An arbitrary third offset for the same rule. 12:05 UTC is 20:05 in Hong Kong.

cases.name: negative-offset-input-renders-as-hong-kong-time
cases.why: A negative offset, which is where a sign error hides. 00:05 in UTC-5 is 05:05 UTC is 13:05 in Hong Kong.

cases.name: crosses-midnight-into-the-next-hong-kong-day
cases.why: 16:30 UTC is 00:30 the FOLLOWING day in Hong Kong. The date rolls forward and the clock reads past midnight — a port that shifted the hour without letting the day carry would print '24:30'.

cases.name: the-first-instant-of-a-hong-kong-day
cases.why: Exactly midnight, and it must read '00:00'. Never '24:00': `hour12: false` alone permits an h24 cycle in some ICU builds, which is one of the things the arithmetic form removes.

cases.name: the-utc-instant-of-hong-kong-midnight
cases.why: 16:00 UTC is the midnight boundary in Hong Kong; one second earlier is still 23:59. Pairs with the row below.

cases.name: hours-are-zero-padded
cases.why: An early-morning first departure. '5:35' would break the column alignment on a departure board.

cases.name: sub-minute-precision-is-truncated-not-rounded
cases.why: 999 milliseconds short of 12:06 still reads '12:05'. Truncation, not rounding: ADR-008 forbids fabricating precision, and a bus that has not yet reached the next minute has not reached it. A port using a rounding formatter shows '12:06' and is a minute optimistic.

cases.name: an-unparseable-string-has-no-clock-time
cases.why: Empty string, not a throw and not 'Invalid Date'. The caller renders an absence; a crash on bad upstream data would take the whole board down.

cases.name: an-out-of-range-date-has-no-clock-time
cases.why: Structurally ISO-shaped but impossible. Must be rejected as unparseable rather than wrapped around into a plausible-looking time.

isStale.doc: Whether a reading is old enough to be shown as stale. Strictly greater than `staleAfterMs` since the feed generated it — the threshold instant itself is still fresh. A row with no `staleAfterMs` argument is stating the shipped default of 90 000 ms; the threshold is served policy (ADR-053), so a port must read the argument rather than a constant of its own. This is a data-quality signal, not an error.

cases.name: exactly-at-the-threshold-is-still-fresh
cases.why: 90 000 ms exactly. The comparison is `>`, not `>=`.

cases.name: feed-timestamp-in-the-future-is-not-stale
cases.why: Upstream clocks run slightly ahead sometimes. A future timestamp yields a negative age, which is never stale.

cases.name: a-served-threshold-makes-a-fresh-reading-stale
cases.why: The same 30 s age that `fresh` calls current, judged against a served 20 s threshold. The row exists to catch the port that reads its own 90 s constant: every other row in this group passes for such a port, because they all happen to agree with the default.

etaLineKey.doc: The rider-facing line an arrival belongs to, as a string two producers can compare: operator + route number + direction, with the service type deliberately absent because a rider does not choose one. An id the grammar cannot parse keys on the whole id, so one odd reading never collapses with another. The literal format is pinned, not just the equivalence classes, because it is a KEY: `dedupeEtas` builds its own key on top of it and the edge indexes a destination table by it, so two spellings of one line would silently drop a destination. Same reason `ids#formatFavoriteRouteKey` is pinned.

cases.name: the-service-type-is-not-part-of-the-line
cases.why: KMB and Citybus split one line into timetable variants (Citybus 969 is listed three times at one pole). The variant is in the route id and must not be in the line.

cases.name: the-direction-is
cases.why: Inbound and outbound are different journeys, so they are different lines.

cases.name: the-operator-is
cases.why: Route 10 exists for both KMB and Citybus, and a merged place can serve both at one kerb.

cases.name: a-gmb-number-that-repeats-across-regions-still-keys-on-the-number
cases.why: GMB numbers repeat, so the government's own route code is what makes the id unique (ADR-047) — and it is a service-type field, so it drops out here. Two GMB services sharing a number are one LINE and are told apart by their pole, which is `dedupeEtas`' job, not this one.

cases.name: an-unparseable-id-keys-on-the-whole-id
cases.why: The least-bad answer when the data is already odd: an unreadable id dedupes only against its own twin rather than collapsing every malformed reading from one operator into a single row. `split(':')` with '' defaults did the latter and dropped the rest.

cases.name: a-literal-pipe-in-the-route-id-keys-on-the-whole-id
cases.why: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW. Nothing escapes a '|' inside a field, so 'KMB:1|2:outbound:1' would have collided with 'KMB:1:2|outbound:1' when the key was built by splitting on ':'. `parseRouteId` rejects both, and an unparseable id keys on the whole id, so they stay two lines. See `dedupeEtas:literal-pipe-in-route-id-collides` for the arrival that disappeared.

etaBoardingKey.doc: The identity of an arrival — a rider line at one boarding point, `<line>|<pole>` — which since WP5-9 is the same unit as a route row's. `dedupeEtas` collapses on it and `applyLiveEtasToStopDetail` falls back to it when a row's exact service-type variant is not the one upstream published, so the literal format is pinned: a fallback keyed differently from the normalisation would attach a reading to a row the wire never gave it to. Same reason `ids#formatFavoriteRouteKey` is pinned.

cases.name: two-poles-of-one-line-are-two-keys
cases.why: The whole point. KMB runs 269D outbound off two poles of Tin Shui Estate, so there are two arrivals to publish and two rows to fill. Compare the next row: it is the SAME line and the keys differ only by the pole.

cases.name: two-service-type-variants-at-one-pole-are-one-key
cases.why: The half that must not change: types 1 and 4 of 269D board at the same kerb, so they are one bus to a rider and one key. Citybus 969 appears three times at one pole for the same reason.

cases.name: an-unparseable-route-id-still-keys-on-its-pole
cases.why: The pole is appended to the fallback line key too, so two unreadable readings at two kerbs stay two arrivals. The pole is deliberately LAST: a pipe in the trailing field can only split a line, never merge two, and canonical ids carry colons and never a pipe (ADR-032).

dedupeEtas.doc: Collapse rider-duplicate arrivals to one reading per line AT ONE BOARDING POINT, keeping the soonest. A rider thinks 'route number + direction', so the key is operator + route number + bound — parsed out of the canonical route id, `etaLineKey` below — plus the canonical id of the POLE the reading's board was called at. The pole joined WP5-9: a place is N poles (ADR-042) and a rider walks to one of them, so one line boarding at two of them is two arrivals and not one. Service-type variants AT one pole still collapse, which is what the rule is for. `args.etas` carries only the four fields the rule reads (routeId, operator, stopId, arrivals); a port should fill the remaining required Eta fields with inert values. `expect` is the surviving routeIds, in output order (insertion order of first sighting).

cases.name: service-type-variants-collapse-keeping-the-sooner
cases.why: KMB indexes the same line under several service types, and both of these are at ONE pole. Two rows, one line; the 12:05 reading wins over the 12:09 one even though it arrived second in the list. This is the collapse the rule exists for and WP5-9 deliberately kept: a rider does not choose a timetable variant, and both buses call at the same kerb.

cases.name: opposite-bounds-are-different-lines
cases.why: The KMB stop feed returns every direction of a route. Inbound and outbound must both survive — they are different journeys.

cases.name: same-number-different-operator-is-two-lines
cases.why: Route '10' exists for both KMB and Citybus. The operator is part of the key.

cases.name: gmb-regional-variants-of-one-number-collapse
cases.why: GMB route numbers repeat across regions, but a stop belongs to exactly one region, so two arrivals at ONE POLE sharing number+bound are always the same route (ADR-047). Collapsing them, keeping the sooner, is intended — not a bug. Across two poles of one place the same shape means the opposite thing; see `one-minibus-number-at-two-poles-is-two-services`.

cases.name: one-line-at-two-poles-keeps-a-reading-for-each
cases.why: THE ROW THIS RULE WAS RE-KEYED FOR (WP5-9), and it exercises both halves at once. Tin Shui Estate, Tin Shui Road: KMB runs 269D outbound off two different poles of one place — service types 1 and 4 at `KMB:C052B4D46E1F48EA` and service type 3 at `KMB:BD53690B9DA1C956`, 20 m away. The two variants at the SAME pole still collapse to the sooner (12:03 beats 12:18, and the survivor keeps the first one's position); the second POLE keeps a reading of its own. Keyed without the pole, all three collapsed into one reading and the second pole's row rendered "no reading right now" while a bus was genuinely due there — measured against the live GMB feed on 2026-07-31, where 68K had buses at both poles of Fu Kin Street 11 s apart and we published one. The unit of an arrival is now the unit of a row (ADR-042: a place is N poles), and the boarding point is the one a rider walks to.

cases.name: one-minibus-number-at-two-poles-is-two-services
cases.why: The case where fusing two poles was not merely unhelpful but WRONG about what a bus is. At Tai On Street, near Sai Wan Ho Station Exit A, `GMB:20:outbound:2002320` boards at `GMB:20000270` for Chai Wan (Fung Yip Street) and `GMB:20:outbound:2002319` boards at `GMB:20009406` for Chai Wan Industrial City. Both are circular, so both are "outbound" on every leg, and the number is the same — direction cannot separate them and neither can the number. Only the pole can. Keyed without it, the second destination was never published at all. `dedupeRoutes` was corrected the same way one wave earlier (ADR-042, WP5-10's correction 11); this is the reading behind the row.

cases.name: a-row-with-no-arrivals-yields-to-one-that-has-them
cases.why: The first sighting is kept provisionally even with an empty arrivals list; a later row with an actual time replaces it.

cases.name: literal-pipe-in-route-id-collides
cases.why: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW (an id containing a literal `|`), and a worked example of what this corpus is FOR. The dedupe key is three fields joined with '|', and nothing escapes a '|' inside a field. When this row was written the key was built by splitting the route id on ':' and defaulting missing fields to '', so 'KMB:1|2:outbound:1' (routeNo '1|2') and 'KMB:1:2|outbound:1' (bound '2|outbound') both flattened to the key 'KMB|1|2|outbound': two distinct lines silently collapsed and one arrival DISAPPEARED from the rider's list. The row was recorded as a knownDefect with that broken expectation. WP1-2's id grammar then landed, `parseRouteId` rejects both of these as unparseable, and an unparseable id keys on the whole id — so they no longer collide and `expect` is now BOTH routeIds. That is the intended lifecycle: the row went red, the expectation was updated in the same commit as the fix, and every other platform's suite will go red until it ports the parser. The row's job now is to keep it fixed. Note the same unescaped-concatenation shape underlies the favourites key `${memberStopId}|${routeId}` (ADR-032, 'canonical ids carry colons, never a pipe').

cases.name: two-different-malformed-ids-stay-two-rows
cases.why: The regression the pipe row's fix had to avoid re-introducing. Two unparseable ids from one operator used to share the key 'KMB||' and collapse into a single row, dropping every reading but one. Keying an unparseable id on the id itself is the least-bad answer when the data is already known to be odd: show the rider both, rather than silently choosing.

cases.name: an-unparseable-id-at-two-poles-stays-two-rows
cases.why: The pole is appended to the fallback key too, not just to the parsed one. An id we cannot read already dedupes only against its own twin (see the two rows above); after WP5-9 that twin also has to be at the same kerb, or one of two odd readings would still vanish. Note the stop id is the key's LAST field, so a pipe inside it can only ever split a line, never merge two — canonical ids carry colons and never a pipe (ADR-032).

formatFare.doc: A single HK$ figure for display. The upstream string is passed through verbatim — no float parsing, no re-rounding, so '6.70' stays '6.70'. A port must not reformat the number.

cases.name: trailing-zero-is-preserved-verbatim
cases.why: Proves the pass-through: a port that parses to a number and reformats would print '$6.7'.

cases.name: blank-fare-yields-a-bare-dollar-sign
cases.why: Recorded so no port 'helpfully' returns an empty string instead. Callers are expected to guard: fareRange/fareStages both skip blanks, so this is unreachable through them.

fareRange.doc: Cheapest/dearest across a set of boarding-stop fares. Compared NUMERICALLY but returned as the ORIGINAL upstream strings, so no float drift reaches the screen. Returns absent when nothing usable is present.

cases.name: compared-numerically-not-lexically
cases.why: The row that catches a string-sorting port: lexically '10.0' < '9.5', numerically it is the maximum.

cases.name: skips-blank-absent-and-non-numeric
cases.why: JSON null is the absent value. The terminus carries no boarding fare, and some rows are blank or junk.

cases.name: first-of-two-equal-values-wins-so-the-string-is-stable
cases.why: '6.70' and '6.7' are numerically equal; neither comparison is strict-greater/less, so the first-seen string is kept for both ends. This is what makes the flat-route collapse in formatFareRange predictable.

formatFareRange.doc: A sectional fare framed high-to-low, mirroring the route's own direction: dearest boarding at the origin, less from each later stage. The arrow is the same U+2192 used by the 'A -> B' route label, spaced on both sides. Collapses to one figure when the fare is flat.

cases.name: high-to-low
cases.why: The separator is space + U+2192 RIGHTWARDS ARROW + space. Copy the character, do not substitute '->'.

cases.name: flat-comparison-is-on-the-string-not-the-number
cases.why: Equality is string equality, so a range of '6.70'/'6.7' would NOT collapse. fareRange guarantees that cannot happen (see its first-of-two-equal-values row); this records the boundary in case something else builds the range.

fareStages.doc: Collapse a route's per-stop sectional fares (array index = seq - 1) into contiguous fare stages. `fromSeq`/`toSeq` are 1-based and inclusive. Consecutive stops with an EQUAL fare merge; a blank, absent or non-numeric fare breaks the run and is itself skipped.

cases.name: two-runs-with-a-fareless-terminus
cases.why: The last stop has no boarding fare, so it produces no stage at all.

cases.name: a-gap-breaks-an-otherwise-equal-run
cases.why: The row that catches a port merging on fare equality alone. Stops 1 and 3 share a fare but stop 2 is blank, so they are TWO stages, not one spanning 1-3. Contiguity is part of the rule.

cases.name: equality-is-on-the-string
cases.why: '6.70' and '6.7' are numerically equal but do not merge. Deliberate: the upstream figure is the source of truth and a change of printed form is a change of fare stage.

estimateChildFare.doc: A LABELLED ESTIMATE, not data: HK open data carries no fares by passenger type. Roughly half the adult fare, rounded to the nearest $0.1, always printed with one decimal. A bounded, deliberate exception to ADR-008 — the UI must always show it as an estimate. Rounding is half-away-from-zero on the tenths (not banker's rounding): a port using Kotlin's Math.rint or Python's round() will disagree on the .x5 cases.

cases.name: half-of-6-7-rounds-up
cases.why: 3.35 -> '3.4'. Half-away-from-zero. This is the case that distinguishes rounding modes.

cases.name: whole-dollars-still-get-one-decimal
cases.why: '17', not '17.0', would be wrong — the one-decimal form is part of the contract so a column of figures aligns.

cases.name: blank-fare-estimates-zero
cases.why: FIXED 2026-07-28. `Number('')` is 0, not NaN, so a `Number.isFinite` guard alone let a *missing* fare through as zero and printed a confident '$0.0' child fare. Absent must stay absent — inventing a figure and labelling it an estimate is what ADR-008 forbids. `parseFareOrUndefined` now rejects blank and whitespace input, so the caller renders nothing.

estimateElderlyFare.doc: A LABELLED ESTIMATE of the Government $2 Scheme fare for 65+/PwD riders, as amended 3 Apr 2026: $2 for adult fares up to $10, otherwise 20% of the adult fare — i.e. max($2, 20%) — and then **capped at the adult fare itself**, because the Scheme caps what a concessionary rider pays and does not invent a charge. The cap is inert above $2 (for any n >= 2, max(2, 0.2n) <= n) and binding below it, which is where the bug was: a $0 interchange section estimated $2.0, a figure no rider is charged and MORE than the adult fare beside it. To one decimal. Requires an eligible/JoyYou Octopus, not cash. Changing the scheme means editing this group and re-porting every platform.

cases.name: a-free-section-costs-a-concessionary-rider-nothing
cases.why: **The bug this group carried until 2026-08-08, reported from the shipping app.** A bus-bus interchange leg is genuinely free — 49X through the Shing Mun Tunnels BBI prices its A5 and A2 sections at $0 — and `max($2, 20%)` turned that into $2.0: a charge that does not exist, printed as an estimate beside an adult fare of $0, i.e. MORE than an adult pays. The Scheme is a cap, not a floor. Wrong on all three renderers at once, because the rule is shared — which is the argument for it being here rather than in a screen.

cases.name: a-fare-below-the-floor-is-never-rounded-up-to-it
cases.why: The general form of the row above, and the one that shows the cap is a rule rather than a special case for zero: a $1.50 fare estimates $1.50, because no concession makes a rider pay more than the adult beside them. `max($2, …)` alone returns $2.0 here.

cases.name: the-cap-is-inert-exactly-where-the-scheme-applies
cases.why: The control that stops the cap being a silent behaviour change: at exactly $2 the two rules agree, so this row would go red if `min` were ever applied to the percentage instead of to the whole expression. Above it, `cheap-fare-pays-the-two-dollar-floor` and the four rows after it are unchanged by the fix — which is the evidence that it is a fix and not a re-tuning.

cases.name: policy-boundary-exactly-ten-dollars
cases.why: The scheme's hinge. 20% of $10 is exactly $2, so the floor and the percentage agree here and the result is $2.0 either way. A port that used a strict inequality on the wrong side still passes this row — the next two rows are what separate them.

cases.name: blank-fare-estimates-the-floor
cases.why: FIXED 2026-07-28. The same blank-input defect, and worse here because `max($2, 0)` is `$2`: a missing fare became a plausible '$2.0' rather than an obvious zero. Now undefined.

formatJourney.doc: Whole-route journey time, always hedged. English prefixes a bare '~' with no space; Chinese uses 約/约 followed by a space. The asymmetry is deliberate typography, not an oversight.

formatHeadway.doc: Typical headway as a coarse range from the GTFS frequency bands — never a fabricated single figure. Collapses when min equals max. The separator is space + U+2013 EN DASH + space; the spacing is deliberate so the dash does not visually fuse with the digits.

cases.name: range-en
cases.why: Separator is ' – ' (U+2013 with a space each side), NOT a hyphen and NOT unspaced.

cases.name: equal-bounds-collapse-en
cases.why: Never 'every 12 – 12 min'.

formatServiceHours.doc: Daily service span on a 24h clock, locale-independent. Same spaced U+2013 EN DASH as formatHeadway. Note what this does NOT do: it performs no wrap normalization, so a past-midnight band value reaches the screen verbatim. Normalizing is the caller's job.

cases.name: past-midnight-end-is-not-normalized
cases.why: FIXED 2026-07-28. '25:35' means 01:35 the next day in the GTFS frequency table (see FreqBand). The formatter now wraps anything at or past 24:00, because this is the display boundary — leaving the wrap to callers is exactly what let a raw '25:35' reach a rider. Unparseable values still pass through untouched, so a surprising upstream string is shown rather than mangled.

cases.name: unparseable-value-passes-through-untouched
cases.why: The wrap only fires on something that actually looks like HH:mm. Anything else is shown as-is rather than mangled or blanked, on the principle that a surprising upstream string should reach someone who can report it. Pinned because the alternative — silently emptying the field — would look like missing data rather than bad data.

classifyRemark.doc: A coarse class for an operator's free-text ETA remark, so the UI can style a timetable-derived arrival differently from a tracked one (ADR-008/036). The feeds carry prose, not codes, so this matches on text in both English and Chinese. English matching is case-insensitive. 'scheduled' is tested first and therefore WINS over 'lastBus' when a remark matches both. Anything unmatched is 'info' — never an error.

cases.name: english-matching-is-case-insensitive
cases.why: Upstream shouts sometimes. The stem is 'schedul', so 'Scheduled'/'SCHEDULE'/'scheduling' all match.

cases.name: blank-en-circular-route-last-bus
cases.why: NAMED BOUNDARY ROW (empty `en`, circular route). Upstream really ships a blank English remark on minor GMB circular services while the Chinese text is populated. The Chinese branch must carry the classification on its own; a port that reads only `en`, or that treats a blank `en` as a hard failure, gets 'info' here and styles a last-bus warning as ordinary information.

remark.zh-Hant: 大角咀(循環線) 尾班車已開出
remark.zh-Hans: 大角咀(循环线) 尾班车已开出

cases.name: blank-en-scheduled-from-chinese-only
cases.why: The same blank-`en` shape for the other class. 未開出 ('not yet departed') is one of the scheduled markers.

cases.name: scheduled-wins-when-a-remark-matches-both
cases.why: Order of evaluation is part of the contract: a scheduled last bus is classed 'scheduled', because 'this is a timetable guess' is the more important caveat.

etaUrgency.doc: How much attention one arrival is owed, as a NAME a renderer turns into a colour — never a colour (ADR-053, applied on the client side of the network this time). It exists because the alternative had already drifted: `apps/mobile/components/EtaBadge.tsx` decided imminence with a literal `parts.value <= 5` — 360 s, since `value` is floored minutes — while the served `warnUnderSec` was 180 and its own comment read "Nothing reads this yet". Both were true, which is how one judgement came to be written down twice. In a live sample of 40 rows, 7 were coloured imminent against the policy. Every row below is stated against the shipped defaults (`dueUnderSec` 60, `warnUnderSec` 180); the last row varies the policy to prove the thresholds are read rather than baked.

cases.name: no-reading-is-none
cases.why: A route with no reading at all. Distinct from departed: the row still exists and still names its route, there is just nothing to count down. A port that treated absent as departed would dim a row that is merely quiet.

cases.name: minus-61s-is-none
cases.why: Past the symmetric due band, so genuinely gone.

cases.name: minus-60s-is-due
cases.why: THE LOWER EDGE, and it is inclusive: `seconds >= -dueUnderSec`. A reading a minute in the past is still shown, because the feed clock and ours disagree by seconds and blanking a stop the rider is standing at is the worse error (see etaView).

cases.name: 59s-is-due
cases.why: Inside the band on the forward side: no figure is shown at all (ADR-008).

cases.name: 60s-is-soon
cases.why: The first second a figure appears, and it is already urgent.

cases.name: 179s-is-soon
cases.why: THE UPPER EDGE of imminence, one second inside the served `warnUnderSec`.

cases.name: 180s-is-normal
cases.why: THE WITNESS ROW. `warnUnderSec` is exclusive, so 180 s is ordinary — and the old literal called this imminent, because floor(180/60) = 3 and 3 <= 5.

cases.name: 359s-is-normal
cases.why: THE SECOND WITNESS, and the widest divergence: floor(359/60) = 5, so `value <= 5` made this imminent too. Nearly six minutes away, coloured as "run".

cases.name: a-served-policy-moves-both-thresholds
cases.why: The point of serving the numbers (ADR-053): the same 200 s reading is `normal` under the shipped 180 s band and `soon` under a served 300 s one. A port that hard-coded either number passes every row above and fails this one.

cases.name: unparseable-arrival-is-none
cases.why: The colour half of etaView's guard row: nothing to be urgent about, so 'none' — a NaN used to compare false against every threshold and land on 'normal' (ADR-142).

etaReadout.doc: The three things every arrival readout is made of — label, urgency, staleness — derived together. They travel together because they must AGREE: the label's "Due" band and the urgency's `due` band are the same `dueUnderSec`, so a caller computing one with a served policy and the other with the default renders the word "Due" in the ordinary colour. Two screens were deriving these by hand before WP4-0 (the Nearby card and the Place detail row); a third renderer would have made three.

cases.name: a-fresh-reading-three-minutes-out
cases.why: The ordinary case: a figure, no urgency, not stale. All three fields at once, which is the point of the function.

cases.name: label-and-urgency-agree-on-the-due-band
cases.why: THE ROW THAT JUSTIFIES THE FUNCTION. A served `dueUnderSec` of 30 must move BOTH halves: the label stops saying "Due" and the urgency stops saying `due` — becoming `soon`, because 45 s is still inside `warnUnderSec`. Before WP4-0 `etaLabelParts` took no such parameter, so this row would have produced label `due` alongside urgency `soon`: the word "Due" rendered in the imminent colour rather than the due one. Worth noting how this row was written: the expectation was hand-typed as `normal` and the suite rejected it, which is the corpus doing its job on the one kind of row a generator cannot check.

cases.name: an-empty-arrivals-array-is-departed-and-not-urgent
cases.why: An `Eta` can arrive carrying no arrivals at all. The readout must be complete anyway — a port that indexed `arrivals[0]` unchecked crashes here.

cases.name: staleness-is-measured-from-the-operators-clock
cases.why: Aged by `dataTimestamp` — when the operator generated the reading — not `observedAt`, so a payload replayed from the offline cache ages honestly instead of looking fresh because we fetched it recently (ADR-058). 91 s against the 90 s default, with a perfectly good arrival still in the future.

remarkView.doc: An operator remark reduced to one locale and classified, or absent when there is nothing to show. Three rules that had been sitting inside `components/RemarkTag.tsx`, reachable only by rendering it: blank-in-this-locale counts as absent; the served `remarkKind` wins; and with no served kind the fallback is `classifyRemark` — THE SAME kernel function the edge calls — which is what makes an offline replay or an older edge indistinguishable from a current one.

cases.name: a-served-kind-is-used-as-given
cases.why: The ordinary path since WP3-4 moved classification to the edge (ADR-053).

cases.name: no-served-kind-falls-back-to-the-same-function-the-edge-calls
cases.why: A payload from the offline cache (ADR-058) or an edge older than the field. The classification must be IDENTICAL, not merely reasonable — one rule, two callers, never two implementations.

cases.name: blank-in-this-locale-is-absent
cases.why: Upstream really sends an empty `en`. Returning it as text puts an empty tag into the layout at a different size, which is a visible gap rather than nothing.

cases.name: the-same-blank-remark-shows-in-chinese
cases.why: The pair to the row above, and the reason blankness is per-locale rather than per-remark: the very same payload has text to show in zh-Hant. A port that checked "is the remark empty" once, for all locales, would drop it in both.

cases.name: no-remark-at-all-is-absent
cases.why: Most readings carry none. Distinct from a blank one only in provenance, identical in effect — which is why both collapse to one absent value rather than two states a renderer would have to tell apart.

cases.name: an-explicit-null-on-the-wire-is-absent
cases.why: THE REGRESSION ROW. The app does no runtime validation (ADR-052 decision 2), so a payload carrying `"remark": null` reaches the kernel as `null` whatever the schema says. The component this replaced read the field as `eta.remark?.[locale]`, where optional chaining absorbed it; the first cut of this function guarded `=== undefined` and threw. Real feeds do not currently send it, so no live sample would have caught this — only a row that states the case.

feedNotice.doc: What a screen says when it has stopped being fed. Precedence is offline -> unreachable -> lastUpdated -> none, because each earlier state explains the later ones. Upstream board refusals are deliberately NOT an input: they are already said per card and per row, and a screen-level sentence could disagree with those (a live round asks each pole separately).

cases.name: a-fresh-board-says-nothing
cases.why: Silence is the ordinary case and must stay silent: a notice that shows while everything works is one riders learn to ignore before the day it matters (ADR-122's lesson about the stale cue crying wolf).

cases.name: a-board-past-the-threshold-says-when-it-was-updated
cases.why: The row this rule exists for. The owner found it with the local Worker down: every time kept counting down and nothing said the data had stopped arriving.

cases.name: exactly-at-the-threshold-is-still-fresh
cases.why: The boundary, on the same side as isStale's: strictly greater than. A port that used >= would announce staleness one tick early on every screen.

cases.name: offline-outranks-a-stale-board
cases.why: Precedence. A rider with no network does not also need telling their data is old — the offline sentence explains the staleness, and two sentences about one situation is worse than one.

cases.name: offline-outranks-an-unreachable-edge
cases.why: Both are true when the network is gone — a fetch that never left the device also failed. Whose problem it is decides which sentence, and it is the rider's.

cases.name: an-unreachable-edge-is-said-even-on-fresh-data
cases.why: A refetch can fail while the readings on screen are still inside the threshold. Staying silent until the data ages would delay the only sentence that tells a rider the screen has stopped moving.

cases.name: no-readings-and-no-trouble-says-nothing
cases.why: A screen still loading, or one with genuinely nothing due, has no freshness to report. Saying 'last updated' with no time to put after it would be worse than silence — the same reason formatClock returns an empty string rather than inventing a value.

cases.name: no-readings-but-offline-still-says-offline
cases.why: The connectivity sentence does not depend on having data: a cold offline start has nothing to be stale, and 'you are offline' is still the thing a rider can act on.

cases.name: an-unparseable-timestamp-is-not-evidence-of-staleness
cases.why: Upstream really does publish fields this app cannot read (the fare sheet's whole defect, ADR-128). A NaN compared against a threshold is false in every direction, so the rule says so explicitly rather than leaning on comparison luck — a port that wrote now - NaN > ms would get silence by accident and a port that wrote the inverse would announce staleness on every screen.

newestBoard.doc: The newest board among the ones a screen drew, or null when it drew none. One rule with four callers, so a tie or an unreadable value cannot be resolved four different ways. Unreadable and absent values are SKIPPED, never folded in as epoch zero.

cases.name: the-newest-of-several-wins
cases.why: The ordinary case, and the reason this is not `[0]`: a payload's order is the feed's, not newest-first, so taking the first board would report an arbitrary one.

cases.name: one-board-is-its-own-newest
cases.why: A single-pole stop, which is most of the dataset.

cases.name: no-boards-at-all-is-null
cases.why: A screen still loading, or one with genuinely nothing due. `feedNotice` reads null as 'no freshness to report' and stays silent rather than saying 'last updated' with nothing to put after it.

cases.name: absent-boards-are-skipped-not-counted
cases.why: A pole with no ETA block is ordinary — a stop can be served by a route with no live feed. Nulls must not make the whole answer null, or one quiet kerb would silence the notice for a place that is otherwise being fed.

cases.name: an-unreadable-timestamp-is-skipped-not-treated-as-epoch-zero
cases.why: Upstream publishes fields this app cannot parse — ADR-128's fare defect is exactly that. A NaN folded into a maximum is harmless, but a NaN coerced to 0 would make one bad field read as 'last updated 08:00' on every screen that touched it, which is a confident lie rather than a silence.

cases.name: only-unreadable-timestamps-is-null
cases.why: The control for the row above: skipping must be able to skip everything and still answer honestly.

cases.name: identical-timestamps-resolve-to-that-instant
cases.why: A batch round stamps every pole with one time (ADR-079), so a tie is the COMMON case rather than an edge one — and it must not depend on iteration order.

cases.name: mixed-offsets-are-compared-as-instants-not-as-strings
cases.why: The row that fails a port comparing strings. 14:19+08:00 and 07:00Z are the same instant; a lexical comparison would pick whichever sorted later and could report a board an hour off. The feed publishes +08:00 and our own frames publish Z.

newestNearbyBoard.doc: The newest board on a nearby list: `newestBoard` over every reading /v1/nearby attached to the cards on screen. The payload comes in whole rather than a list of timestamps because WHICH field is the board's clock is a domain decision — dataTimestamp, the operator's clock, never observedAt, which is when we fetched it and is fresh on every refetch for ever.

cases.name: the-newest-board-across-two-cards-wins
cases.why: A nearby list is several places, each with its own boards, and a rider reads one screen. The freshest one is what 'last updated' means to them.

cases.name: a-card-with-no-readings-contributes-nothing
cases.why: A place whose every board is quiet is ordinary, and it must not silence the notice for the places beside it that ARE being fed.

cases.name: no-cards-at-all-is-null
cases.why: The first paint, before any answer. Null keeps the notice silent rather than saying 'last updated' with nothing to put after it.

cases.name: the-clock-is-the-operators-not-ours
cases.why: The whole reason this adapter exists. observedAt is stamped by our own layer on every fetch, so a board that stopped publishing at lunchtime still has a fresh one — a screen that read it would say 'last updated' about a feed that has been silent for hours. This case fails if anyone swaps the field.

newestPlaceBoard.doc: The newest board across one or more place documents: Place detail's one, and every place Favourites resolved its saved poles to. A list rather than a single document because Favourites fans out one query per saved pole, and 'the newest board on this screen' is a fact about the screen, not about whichever query answered last. Rows with no reading contribute nothing.

cases.name: the-newest-board-across-two-places-wins
cases.why: Favourites' shape: several places, fetched independently, drawn as one list.

cases.name: a-row-with-no-reading-contributes-nothing
cases.why: A place is usually a mix: one route with a live board and several that only have a timetable. The timetabled rows are absent, not epoch zero, so the live board is what the screen reports.

cases.name: no-places-at-all-is-null
cases.why: A rider with nothing saved, or a screen whose first query has not resolved. Silence, not a claim.

cases.name: the-clock-is-the-operators-not-ours
cases.why: The same trap as the nearby adapter's, and it is worth pinning on both: observedAt is ours and always fresh, dataTimestamp is the operator's and is the only one that can say a feed has stopped.
